analysis.one_liner: Phases out hydraulic fracturing for oil and gas nationwide, with tighter immediate limits near homes and schools.
analysis.headline: The first-ever House bill to ban fracking nationwide never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it sat in committee for the remaining 11 months of the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop the federal government from approving any expansion of fracking or fracked gas and oil infrastructure, including new pipelines, export terminals, and gas power plants. It would immediately shut down fracked wells operating within 2,500 feet of a home, school, or other occupied building, and it would ban fracking on all land in the United States, onshore and offshore, by 2025. It also directs the Labor Department to set up a committee to recommend ways to protect workers and communities in oil and gas regions during the phaseout.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 17 million Americans who live within a mile of an oil or gas well or related facility, especially low-income communities and communities of color that the bill's findings say are disproportionately exposed to fracking pollution, along with anyone affected by water contamination, air pollution, earthquakes linked to wastewater injection, and methane-driven climate change. Fossil fuel workers would be promised a transition, though the bill only creates a committee to make recommendations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living near fracked wells and pipelines

how_it_helps.text: The bill bans fracking on all onshore and offshore land in the United States beginning January 1, 2025, and bars federal agencies from approving permits for new fracking operations or fracked-gas and oil infrastructure, including pipelines, LNG export terminals, and gas power plants.
Starting February 1, 2021, it would immediately revoke federal permits and stop production at any fracked well found to be operating within 2,500 feet of a home, school, or other inhabited structure.
The bill requires the EPA to survey all oil and gas wells to identify where fracking is used, including how close wells are to homes and schools and any known health and safety violations.

The bill's findings cite research linking fracking to drinking water contamination, air pollution, high-risk pregnancies, and low birth weight, and note that more than 17 million people live within a mile of a well or related facility.

It directs the Department of Labor to create a Just Transition Committee, consulting organized labor and frontline communities, to recommend how to protect the health, safety, and prosperity of oil- and gas-producing regions during the phaseout.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers, pipeline and LNG terminal developers, and gas power plant owners would lose the ability to expand and, by 2025, to frack at all. Workers and local economies in oil- and gas-producing regions would bear the transition costs, though the bill's Just Transition Committee only makes recommendations — it does not itself guarantee wages, pensions, healthcare, or retraining. Households could face higher energy prices as fracked gas supply is phased out faster than replacement energy is built.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers and drilling-region workers

drawbacks.text: The bill would shut down wells near inhabited structures within roughly a year of passage and ban all fracking within five years, a pace faster than wind, solar, storage, and grid upgrades can be built, raising the risk of higher energy prices and supply disruptions for households that rely on natural gas for heating and electricity.

The oil and gas industry directly employs many workers and supports local economies in states like Texas, Pennsylvania, Oklahoma, and North Dakota; the bill's Just Transition Committee is only empowered to make recommendations to Congress and does not itself guarantee incomes, healthcare, pensions, or new jobs for those workers.

The immediate revocation provision takes effect February 1, 2021, leaving less than a year for regulators, companies, and communities to adjust, and applies to existing wells already operating near homes and schools, not just new ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and climate case for phasing out fracking is substantial: the bill's own findings document water contamination, air pollution, pregnancy risks, earthquakes, and methane emissions, and more than a dozen states including New York and Vermont had already banned fracking. But the bill's speed is a real cost. Shutting wells near homes within a year and banning fracking nationwide within five would strain energy supply and hit drilling-region workers hard, and the bill offers a transition committee rather than actual guarantees of income, healthcare, or retraining for them. A slower phaseout paired with binding worker protections would have traded less immediate health benefit for less disruption; this bill chose speed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to an Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee three weeks later, and neither committee ever took it up before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced the Fracking Ban Act on February 12, 2020, with Rep. Darren Soto as co-lead, the first bill to propose banning fracking nationwide.

The bill was referred to the Natural Resources Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, which split jurisdiction and meant both committees had to act before the bill could reach the floor.
On February 21, 2020, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and no further action was ever recorded.
Twenty-one House Democrats cosponsored the bill, out of 231 House Democrats; no Republicans did.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with the bill still parked in committee, so it received no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote, and it died automatically.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers, pipeline developers, and LNG export companies were better off: with the bill dead, federal permits for fracking expansion and fracked-gas infrastructure continued to be issued, and no federal limits on well proximity to homes were imposed. Communities living near fracked wells saw none of the bill's protections take effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers and pipeline companies

for.name: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fracking Ban Act and recruited cosponsors for it.

against.name: Raúl Grijalva
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee of primary referral that never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill during the 11 remaining months of the Congress.

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the second committee of referral that never took up the bill before the Congress ended.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Producers, pipeline and LNG export developers
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal fracking bans and lobbied to preserve permitting for fracking and fracked-gas infrastructure; the industry's principal trade association is cited in the bill's own findings on the share of wells that would be fracked.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, but the bill's support was entirely Democratic — all 21 cosponsors were Democrats out of 231 in the House, and no Republican signed on.

industries.note: The bill would end fracking nationwide by 2025 and immediately shut wells near homes and schools. The industry's interest in continuing fracking runs against residents' interest in clean water, clean air, and reduced methane emissions.

industries.industry: Pipeline, LNG export, and gas power plant developers
industries.note: Federal agencies could approve no new fracked-gas or oil infrastructure, including pipelines, export terminals, and gas power plants. These projects are the main channel through which expanded fracking reaches communities, and several have involved land seized from property owners.

With fracked gas phased out, the market for wind, solar, and storage expands; the bill's findings argue these technologies exist at commercial scale and at or below the cost of fossil fuels. Cheaper, cleaner power serves the public interest alongside the industry's.

Fracking contractors and service firms would lose their core business, and the workers they employ in drilling regions would need new jobs. The bill creates a committee to study a just transition but does not itself fund one.
